segments.english: He used to say: The more flesh, the more worms. The more property, the more anxiety. The more wives, the more witchcraft. The more maidservants, the more lewdness. The more male slaves, the more robbery. The more Torah, the more life. The more sitting in study, the more wisdom. The more counsel, the more understanding. The more charity, the more peace. One who has acquired a good name has acquired it for himself. One who has acquired for himself words of Torah has acquired for himself the life of the world to come.

tokens.note: הָיָה אוֹמֵר: 'was saying', the habitual past in rabbinic Hebrew: 'used to say'.
מַרְבֶּה: hifil participle of רבה, 'one who increases'; the saying is a pair of such participles, 'the more ..., the more ...'.
רִמָּה: 'worm, maggot', especially the worm of the grave (Jastrow); Bartenura: the worm is as painful to the dead as a needle in living flesh.
כְשָׁפִים: 'sorceries, witchcraft'; the plural.
יְשִׁיבָה: 'sitting', here sitting in study or in the academy.
צְדָקָה: 'charity', also 'righteousness'; see note.
קָנָה: 'acquired'; the pack links it to BDB 'Kanah' (a place name), a different word; no sense given.
הַבָּא: 'the coming', the qal participle of בוא with the article; Jastrow בָּא III: עוֹלָם הַבָּא 'the world to come'.

grammar: מַרְבֶּה is a hifil masculine singular participle ('one who increases'). The saying runs on one pattern, מַרְבֶּה X מַרְבֶּה Y, and the English gives it as 'the more X, the more Y'; the participle carries no 'if' or 'then'.

The first five pairs set a possession against its cost (flesh and worms, property and anxiety, wives and witchcraft, maidservants and lewdness, slaves and robbery); the next four set a good against its reward (Torah and life, study and wisdom, counsel and understanding, charity and peace). The list is closed by two sentences with קָנָה, the perfect used for a general truth.

דְאָגָה (anxiety), כְשָׁפִים (sorceries, plural of כֶּשֶׁף) and זִמָּה (lewdness) are all biblical words (Prov 12:25; 2 Kgs 9:22; Lev 18:17); the pack's BDB entries for זִמָּה and עֶבֶד are proper names with the same consonants, and Jastrow's entry for רָבָה is only a cross-reference.
In קָנָה לוֹ, the preposition with suffix לוֹ is a dative of advantage ('for himself'); in לְעַצְמוֹ the noun 'bone, self' is used as the reflexive.
הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא is a noun with an article plus a participle with an article, 'the world that comes'; decisions.md fixes it as 'the world to come'.
segments.note: מַרְבֶּה is given as 'the more ...' to keep the brevity of the sayings. בָּשָׂר is rendered 'flesh' as in Bartenura (one who eats and drinks until he is fat); the English does not decide whether the worms of the grave or of the body are meant. יְשִׁיבָה: 'sitting', that is, sitting in session or in the academy (Bartenura: many disciples gather to hear his reasoning); I keep the literal word. In this reading the clause is 'more sitting, more wisdom', and Bartenura notes that others read 'one who increases yeshivah increases wisdom', which is what our text has. צְדָקָה: 'charity' (giving), the sense of the later usage; Bartenura quotes Isaiah 32:17, where the word is 'righteousness', so the English keeps 'charity' while the wider sense is recorded here.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: one who eats and drinks until he is fat and fleshy increases worms on himself in the grave, and the worm is as painful to the dead as a needle in living flesh. He adds that this tanna teaches that every increase is harmful to a person except increase of Torah, wisdom and charity.

Bartenura: the anxiety is lest the king's household (the government) rob him or bandits come upon him and kill him. He cites a pious man who prayed to be saved from 'scattering of the soul', which meant having many goods scattered in many places so that one must scatter one's mind to think of this place and that.

Bartenura: the order of the list is a sequence of causes: first a man adorns himself, eats and drinks and grows fleshy; then he seeks wealth; with wealth enough to support many women he takes many wives; each wife needs a maidservant; and a large household needs fields and vineyards and slaves to work them.
Bartenura: 'more Torah, more life' because it is written (Deuteronomy 30:20) 'for it is your life and the length of your days'.

Bartenura comments on the order 'the more wisdom, the more yeshivah': one who increases wisdom gives reasons for his words and his arguments settle in the hearts of the hearers, so that disciples gather to him (2:7:6). The base text has the reverse order, which Bartenura records as the reading of others; the English follows the base text.

Bartenura: many disciples gather to hear his arguments. He notes the reading 'more sitting, more wisdom' (the reading of our text): one who has many disciples is sharpened by them, and they increase and add to his wisdom.
Bartenura: 'increases counsel' means one who takes counsel often.
Bartenura: 'understanding' is to understand one thing from another, from the counsel that his advisers give him.
Bartenura: the support for charity and peace is Isaiah 32:17, 'and the work of righteousness shall be peace'.
Rabbeinu Yonah: one who gives charity is loved by those who benefit from his money and so increases peace in the world; one who advises others to give also has it counted to his credit.

Rabbeinu Yonah: a good name is for himself and he will not leave it to others, unlike the one who increases property, who at death leaves it and goes without any of the desirable things he gained from it.

apparatus: No variant readings are recorded between the witnesses for this mishnah.
Bartenura (2:7:6) knows both orders, 'increases wisdom, increases sitting' and 'increases sitting, increases wisdom'; the base text has the second.
Isaiah 32:17 and Deuteronomy 30:20 are quoted by Bartenura, not by the mishnah.

segments.english: Rabban Yohanan son of Zakkai received from Hillel and from Shammai. He used to say: If you have learned much Torah, do not claim credit for yourself, for to this end you were created. Rabban Yohanan son of Zakkai had five disciples, and these are they: Rabbi Eliezer son of Hyrcanus, Rabbi Yehoshua son of Hananiah, Rabbi Yose the Priest, Rabbi Shimon son of Netanel, and Rabbi Elazar son of Arach. He used to enumerate their praises: Rabbi Eliezer son of Hyrcanus, a plastered cistern that does not lose a drop. Rabbi Yehoshua son of Hananiah, happy is she who bore him. Rabbi Yose the Priest, a pious man. Rabbi Shimon son of Netanel, a fearer of sin. And Rabbi Elazar son of Arach, a spring gathering strength. He used to say: If all the sages of Israel were in one pan of a scale, and Eliezer son of Hyrcanus in the other pan, he would outweigh them all. Abba Shaul says in his name: If all the sages of Israel were in one pan of a scale, and Rabbi Eliezer son of Hyrcanus also with them, and Rabbi Elazar son of Arach in the other pan, he would outweigh them all.

tokens.note: רַבָּן: 'our master', a title of the heads of the Sanhedrin.
קִבֵּל: piel perfect of קבל, 'received (the tradition)'.
הַרְבֵּה: hifil infinitive absolute of רבה, 'much, abundantly'.
תַּחֲזִיק: hifil imperfect of חזק; with טוֹבָה it means 'to take credit'.
טוֹבָה: 'goodness, favor'; in אַל תַּחֲזִיק טוֹבָה, 'do not give yourself credit'.
נוֹצָרְתָּ: nifal perfect of יצר, 'were formed'; the sense is 'were created'.
הָיוּ: qal perfect 3rd plural of הָיָה; with לוֹ it states possession.
וְאֵלּוּ: 'and these'; the Mishnaic form of the demonstrative.
הֵן: 'they', the Mishnaic 3rd plural pronoun, used here of masculine persons.
וְרַבִּי: 'and Rabbi' (my master), the title of a sage.
מוֹנֶה: qal participle of מנה, 'counting, enumerating'; with הָיָה, 'used to enumerate'.
שִׁבְחָן: 'their praise', with the Mishnaic 3rd plural suffix -ָן, used for masculine referents (here the five disciples) as for feminine.
בּוֹר: 'cistern, pit'; the pack's Jastrow entry (בּוּר I) is for another word, so no sense is given.

סוּד: 'plastered', the qal passive participle of סוד 'to plaster' (Rabbeinu Yonah: סָדוּ אוֹתוֹ בְּסִיד 'they plastered it with lime'). Bartenura reads סוּד and rejects סִיד 'lime' (the Vilna spelling). The pack's lexicon has only סוֹד 'council, counsel' (BDB) and 'foundation' (Jastrow), other words, so no sense is given.
מְאַבֵּד: piel participle of אבד, 'causes to be lost'.
טִפָּה: 'a drop'.
אַשְׁרֵי: 'happy, blessed' (an exclamation); the pack's Jastrow entry is only a cross-reference, so no sense is given.
יוֹלַדְתּוֹ: feminine participle (construct) of ילד with a 3rd masculine suffix: 'she who bore him'.
חָסִיד: 'pious'; Bartenura: one who acts beyond the line of the law.
יְרֵא: construct of the adjective 'fearing'.
מַעְיָן: 'spring, fountain'.
הַמִּתְגַּבֵּר: hitpael participle of גבר with the article, 'the one who grows strong'.
מֹאזְנַיִם: dual, 'a pair of scales'.
מַכְרִיעַ: hifil participle of כרע, 'makes the scale tip', that is 'outweighs'.
מִשְּׁמוֹ: 'in his name', that is, in Rabban Yohanan's name (Bartenura).
אַף: 'also, even'.
עִמָּהֶם: 'with them'; the preposition עִם with its plural suffix.

grammar: קִבֵּל (piel of קבל) is the technical verb of transmission: 'received (the tradition)'. It has no stated object in the mishnah.

אִם לָמַדְתָּ תּוֹרָה הַרְבֵּה: a conditional with the perfect (אִם plus qatal), and הַרְבֵּה, the hifil infinitive absolute of רבה, used as an adverb after the object; אַל תַּחֲזִיק is a negative command with hifil yiqtol of חזק.
חֲמִשָּׁה תַלְמִידִים הָיוּ לוֹ: possession is expressed by הָיָה plus ל ('five disciples were to him'); the following לְרַבָּן יוֹחָנָן בֶּן זַכַּאי repeats the owner by name.

הוּא הָיָה מוֹנֶה שִׁבְחָן and הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר: הָיָה with a participle is the habitual past ('used to enumerate', 'used to say'); the suffix -ָן in שִׁבְחָן is the Mishnaic 3rd person plural, used for masculine as for feminine referents: 'their praises'.

Each praise is a nominal clause without a verb: name, then predicate (בּוֹר סוּד ..., אַשְׁרֵי יוֹלַדְתּוֹ, חָסִיד, יְרֵא חֵטְא, מַעְיָן הַמִּתְגַּבֵּר); יְרֵא חֵטְא is a construct chain of adjective and noun.
מַכְרִיעַ אֶת כֻּלָּם: hifil participle of כרע, 'tilts the scale against them all'; the weighing is expressed by a conditional with the plural יִהְיוּ and the dual מֹאזְנַיִם, 'a pair of scales'.
segments.note: קִבֵּל מֵהִלֵּל וּמִשַּׁמָּאי: the English leaves the object unsaid, as in the Hebrew; the sense is 'received the tradition'. אַל תַּחֲזִיק טוֹבָה לְעַצְמְךָ: 'do not claim credit for yourself' (Bartenura: do not say 'I have learned much Torah'; he left no Scripture, Mishnah, halakhah or aggadah unlearned). The literal 'do not hold goodness for yourself' is kept in the literal line. בּוֹר סוּד: סוּד is the passive participle of סוד 'to plaster': 'a plastered cistern'. Bartenura says that this is the reading, not בּוֹר סִיד 'a cistern of lime' (the Vilna spelling), and explains 'like a cistern coated with lime'; Rambam: 'like a lined cistern that does not lose its water'. The English follows the base text as both explain it. חָסִיד: 'a pious man'; Bartenura: one who acts beyond the line of the law. יְרֵא חֵטְא: 'a fearer of sin'; Bartenura: one who is strict with himself and forbids himself permitted things for fear of sin. מַעְיָן הַמִּתְגַּבֵּר: 'a spring gathering strength': Bartenura says his heart is wide and he adds arguments and reasons from his own mind. אַבָּא שָׁאוּל אוֹמֵר מִשְּׁמוֹ: Bartenura reads 'in his name' as in the name of Rabban Yohanan; and he writes that Abba Shaul does not dispute the first teacher, but both sayings are the Rabban's, and both are true, since for knowledge and memory Rabbi Eliezer outweighs all and for sharpness and argument Rabbi Elazar son of Arach does.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: 'do not claim credit' means do not say 'I have learned much Torah'. Rabban Yohanan said this because he left no Scripture, Mishnah, halakhah or aggadah that he had not learned (Sukkah 28a, Bava Batra 134a).
Bartenura: the reading is בּוֹר סוּד, not בּוֹר סִיד ('a cistern of lime'); that is, like a cistern coated (plastered) with lime.
Bartenura: 'does not lose a drop' means that he does not forget a single thing from his learning.

Bartenura: 'happy is she who bore him': he is blessed with good traits so that everyone says 'happy is the woman who bore him'. Another explanation: his mother caused him to be wise, going round all the study-houses of her city and asking them to pray that the child in her womb should be wise, and from the day he was born she did not take his cradle out of the study-house, so that only words of Torah should enter his ears.
Bartenura: חָסִיד is one who acts beyond the line of the law.

Bartenura: a fearer of sin is one who is strict with himself and forbids himself things that are permitted, out of fear that he might come to sin; otherwise what is the distinction, for even an unlearned person can be a fearer of sin?
Bartenura: 'a spring gathering strength': his heart is broad and he adds argument and reasoning from his own mind.
Bartenura: 'in his name' means in the name of Rabban Yohanan son of Zakkai.

Bartenura: he has found it written that Abba Shaul does not disagree with the first teacher, that both statements were said by Rabban Yohanan, and both are true: for breadth of knowledge and memory, Rabbi Eliezer tips the scale; for keenness and argument, Rabbi Elazar son of Arach does.

Rambam: Rabbi Eliezer was praised for memory, as like a lined cistern that does not lose its water; Rabbi Yehoshua for the excellence of his character traits, by which a man is happy, honored and loved by most of the world, hence 'happy is she who bore him'; Rabbi Yose for his good character and his intellectual virtues; Rabbi Shimon for fear of sin, which is diligence and effort in the affairs of the good and guarding oneself from evil; Rabbi Elazar son of Arach for good understanding, every deep matter being light for him and his insight adding to the matter.
Rabbeinu Yonah: 'happy' said without more means that he was blessed in all the blessed traits, great in wisdom and in order in his traits and in all his affairs.

segments.english: He said to them: Go out and see which is the right way that a person should cling to. Rabbi Eliezer says: A good eye. Rabbi Yehoshua says: A good companion. Rabbi Yose says: A good neighbor. Rabbi Shimon says: One who sees what is to come. Rabbi Elazar says: A good heart. He said to them: I prefer the words of Elazar son of Arach to your words, for your words are included in his words. He said to them: Go out and see which is the evil way that a person should keep far from. Rabbi Eliezer says: An evil eye. Rabbi Yehoshua says: An evil companion. Rabbi Yose says: An evil neighbor. Rabbi Shimon says: One who borrows and does not repay. One who borrows from a person is as one who borrows from the Omnipresent, blessed be He, as it is said (Psalms 37): The wicked one borrows and does not repay, but the Righteous One is gracious and gives. Rabbi Elazar says: An evil heart. He said to them: I prefer the words of Elazar son of Arach to your words, for your words are included in his words.

grammar: The question is asked twice: אֵיזוֹהִי דֶרֶךְ יְשָׁרָה שֶׁיִּדְבַּק בָּהּ הָאָדָם and אֵיזוֹהִי דֶרֶךְ רָעָה שֶׁיִּתְרַחֵק מִמֶּנָּה הָאָדָם. אֵיזוֹהִי is 'which is' (the feminine of the Mishnaic interrogative, agreeing with דֶרֶךְ, which is feminine); שֶׁיִּדְבַּק and שֶׁיִּתְרַחֵק are relative clauses with the imperfect (qal of דבק, hitpael of רחק) of purpose or fitness.

The answers are nominal clauses in a fixed frame: name + אוֹמֵר + noun + adjective (עַיִן טוֹבָה, חָבֵר טוֹב, שָׁכֵן טוֹב, לֵב טוֹב), and the opposites with רָע/רָעָה. The adjective agrees with the noun in gender, so עַיִן, which is feminine, takes טוֹבָה and רָעָה.

הָרוֹאֶה אֶת הַנּוֹלָד: 'the one who sees the born' has a qal participle with the article and a nifal participle with the article (the object marker אֶת before it); the idiom means to see what will come to be. Its answer-partner is הַלֹּוֶה וְאֵינוֹ מְשַׁלֵּם, a participle plus a negative participial clause with אֵין and a suffix.

רוֹאֶה אֲנִי אֶת דִּבְרֵי אֶלְעָזָר ... מִדִּבְרֵיכֶם: the participle comes before the pronoun, the usual Mishnaic order ('I see'); the comparative מִן means 'rather than'. שֶׁבִּכְלָל דְּבָרָיו דִּבְרֵיכֶם is a nominal clause with a fronted prepositional phrase.

Rabbi Shimon's second saying quotes Psalm 37:21 (לֹוֶה רָשָׁע וְלֹא יְשַׁלֵּם, וְצַדִּיק חוֹנֵן וְנוֹתֵן), introduced by שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר, 'as it is said'; the verse is in biblical Hebrew with participles (חוֹנֵן, 'gracious', and נוֹתֵן, 'giving').
segments.note: עַיִן טוֹבָה / עַיִן רָעָה: a 'good eye' is contentment with what one has (Bartenura, Rambam); Rabbeinu Yonah, who is not normative, reads it as generosity. The English keeps the idiom and gives the sense here. הָרוֹאֶה אֶת הַנּוֹלָד: 'one who sees what is to come': Bartenura says he looks at what will be and weighs the loss of a commandment against its reward, and the gain of a transgression against its loss; Rambam says he reflects on the outcome of his affairs. The literal is 'one who sees that which is born'. רוֹאֶה אֲנִי: 'I prefer', literally 'I see'; Rambam says it means 'chooses and discerns'. אֶחָד הַלֹּוֶה ... כְּלֹוֶה: 'one who borrows ... is as one who borrows': the comparison makes the debt to a person a debt to God. הַמָּקוֹם: 'the Omnipresent', literally 'the Place' (decisions.md). וְצַדִּיק חוֹנֵן וְנוֹתֵן: in Psalm 37:21 this is the righteous person who gives to others; Bartenura (and Rambam) read the 'righteous one' as God, who is gracious to the lender and gives him what the borrower did not repay, so that the borrower remains a debtor to the Omnipresent. The English follows them: 'the Righteous One'. Bartenura (2:9:6) explains why the evil way is asked about separately: the opposite of every good trait is not necessarily evil, so a second question was needed.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: a good eye is one who is content with what he has, does not seek superfluous things, and is not envious when he sees that his fellows have more than he.
Bartenura: a good companion is one who rebukes him when he sees him doing something improper.
Bartenura: a good neighbor is to be found near him by day and by night, whereas a good companion is not near him at all times.
Bartenura: one who sees what is to be looks ahead at what will come, and so weighs the loss of a commandment against its reward and the reward of a transgression against its loss.

Bartenura: the heart moves all the other powers and is the source of all actions; although actions have their own organs, the power that rouses all movements is in the heart, so Rabbi Elazar said 'a good heart', and so Rabban Yohanan preferred his words.

Bartenura: the second question was needed because he did not understand from their first answers that the evil way is the opposite of the good way, since not everything good has an evil opposite: ḥasidut is good, but one who is not pious and stands on the law of the Torah is not evil; and the seeking of surplus might not be called evil as it harms no one.

Bartenura: the one who borrows and does not repay is the opposite of 'one who sees what is to be', for if he does not repay he will find no one to lend to him and will be left hungry. He did not simply say 'one who does not see what is to be', because one who does not foresee might still avoid mishap by saving himself when it comes.

Bartenura: 'the righteous one' is the Holy One, blessed be He, who is the righteous one of the world, gracious and giving to the lender what the borrower borrowed from him and did not repay, so that the borrower remains a debtor to the Omnipresent.

Rambam: a good eye is contentment with what a person has, one of the virtues of character, and an evil eye is its opposite, the belittling of things and eagerness for more; 'sees what is to be' is the thought a man gives to the outcome of his affairs and livelihood; the borrower who does not repay is a counter-example, a mean trait; 'the righteous one is gracious and gives' is God, who repays the lender; 'I see his words' is 'I choose and discern'; and a good heart means good actions, the middle path of the virtues, and includes contentment, love of the good and the other virtues, while an evil heart includes all the vices.
Rabbeinu Yonah: the speaker of 'he said to them' is Rabban Yohanan son of Zakkai to his disciples.

apparatus: Psalm 37:21: לֹוֶה רָשָׁע וְלֹא יְשַׁלֵּם וְצַדִּיק חוֹנֵן וְנוֹתֵן.

segments.english: They said three things. Rabbi Eliezer says: Let your fellow's honor be as dear to you as your own, and do not be quick to anger. And repent one day before your death. And warm yourself at the fire of the sages, and beware of their coals, lest you be burned; for their bite is the bite of a fox, their sting is the sting of a scorpion, their whisper is the whisper of a fiery serpent, and all their words are like coals of fire.
segments.literal: they said three things. Rabbi Eliezer says: let-be honor-of your-fellow dear on-you like-yours, and-not be easy to-anger. and-repent day one before your-death. and-be warming-yourself opposite their-fire of sages, and-be careful in-their-coals that-not you-be-burned, that their-bite bite-of fox, and-their-sting sting-of scorpion, and-their-whisper whisper-of saraph, and-all their-words like-coals-of fire

tokens.note: אָמְרוּ: qal perfect 3rd plural.
יְהִי: jussive of הָיָה, 'let ... be'.
תְּהִי: jussive of הָיָה; with אַל it forbids: 'do not be'.
שׁוּב: qal imperative of שׁוב, 'turn back, repent'.
הֱוֵי: the Mishnaic imperative of הָיָה, 'be'; with a participle it asks for a continued act.
כְּנֶגֶד: 'opposite, in front of'.
אוּרָן: 'their fire': אוּר 'fire' (with shureq, distinct from אוֹר 'light'); the suffix -ָן is the Mishnaic 3rd plural, referring to the sages.
תִכָּוֶה: nifal imperfect of כוה, 'be burned'.
שׁוּעָל: 'fox'; Bartenura: its bite is hard to heal because its teeth are thin and crooked.
שָׂרָף: a burning, venomous serpent (Jastrow שָׂרָף I); Bartenura: its breath burns as it whispers, or it will not heed a charmer.

grammar: הֵם אָמְרוּ שְׁלשָׁה דְבָרִים: 'they' are the five disciples, each of whom said three things (Rabbeinu Yonah; Bartenura: three things on conduct and character, always on their lips); the three of Rabbi Eliezer follow (Bartenura counts them in 2:10:2; Rambam holds that the third, on the sages' fire, is a saying he reported from another).

יְהִי and תְּהִי are jussive and imperfect of הָיָה used as imperatives; וֶהֱוֵי is the imperative with a conjunction. The pairs וֶהֱוֵי מִתְחַמֵּם and וֶהֱוֵי זָהִיר govern a participle and an adjective: 'be warming yourself', 'be careful'.
שֶׁלֹּא תִכָּוֶה: שֶׁלֹּא with the nifal imperfect of כוה, 'that you not be burned'.

The ending -ָן in גַּחַלְתָּן, נְשִׁיכָתָן, עֲקִיצָתָן, לְחִישָׁתָן and אוּרָן (and שִׁבְחָן in 2:8) is the 3rd person plural suffix of Mishnaic Hebrew ('their'), used for masculine as for feminine referents; here it refers to the sages (חֲכָמִים).
Each of the three comparisons is a construct chain, 'the bite of a fox', 'the sting of a scorpion', 'the whisper of a saraph', in which the second member names a creature whose attack is feared.
segments.note: הֵם: the disciples of Rabban Yohanan, each of whom said three things (Rabbeinu Yonah; Bartenura's 'these three things were always on their lips'); the English keeps 'They'. אוּרָן: אוּר 'fire' (with shureq), distinct from אוֹר 'light'; the English 'fire' is the plain sense. שׁוּעָל: 'fox' (Bartenura describes its teeth as thin and crooked, so the bite is hard to heal). לְחִישָׁה: 'whisper, spell'; Bartenura glosses it as דִּבּוּרָן, 'their speech'. שָׂרָף: 'saraph, fiery serpent'. כְּנֶגֶד, rendered 'at', is literally 'opposite'; Rabbeinu Yonah glosses 'near'. The English takes שֶׁלֹּא תִכָּוֶה as 'lest you be burned' and the following שֶׁ clause as the reason.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: they spoke about conduct (derekh eretz), moral discipline and character traits, because on what is forbidden and permitted, exempt and liable, they said many things; or else, these three things were always on their lips.

Bartenura: 'when will your fellow's honor be as dear as your own? When you are not easily angered, for otherwise you cannot avoid slighting your fellow's honor.' That is one saying; repenting a day before death is the second; warming yourself at the sages' fire is the third.
Bartenura: since no one knows when he will die, he should repent today in case he dies tomorrow.
Bartenura: 'be careful of their coals' means do not treat them lightly.
Bartenura: 'lest you be burned' means lest you be punished through them.
Bartenura: the bite of a fox is hard to heal because its teeth are thin, crooked and twisted, and the physician must cut the flesh with a scalpel and widen the bite.
Bartenura: the sting of a scorpion is more severe than the bite of a snake.
Bartenura: לְחִישָׁתָן means their speech (דִּבּוּרָן).

Bartenura: the whisper of a saraph is like the breath that comes from the mouth of the saraph, which burns while it whispers. Another explanation: this saraph does not accept a charm, unlike other snakes (Psalm 58:6, 'that will not hear the voice of charmers'); so a disciple of the sages, if you provoke him and then come to appease him, does not accept appeasement.

Rambam: 'do not be easily angered' means do not prepare yourself for anger and irritability; the sages exaggerated in condemning anger, the strongest saying being that whoever is angry is as one who worships an idol.

Rambam: a man does not know when he will die, so all his days should be in repentance. He also says that 'warm yourself at the fire of the sages' is not among this sage's own sayings but something he heard from another and reported, so it is not counted among his own words; its meaning is that when you associate with the wise you should draw near only as they draw you near, as one who warms himself at a fire sits at a distance and benefits from its heat, and is burned if he comes too close.

apparatus: 2:10.17 spelling: Vilna reads לכעוס; base לִכְעֹס.
A stray 'שלשה' appears in the Vilna witness with no counterpart in the base (the base reads שְׁלשָׁה at 2:10.3).
Rabbeinu Yonah (2:10:9) notes that the copyist thinks a word is missing at 'and all their words'.
Psalm 58:6 is quoted by Bartenura, not by the mishnah.

segments.english: Rabbi Yehoshua says: The evil eye, the evil impulse, and hatred of people remove a person from the world.
segments.literal: Rabbi Yehoshua says: eye the-evil, and-impulse the-evil, and-hatred-of the-creatures, remove-they ACC the-person from the-world

tokens.note: עַיִן: 'eye', a feminine noun; Rabbeinu Yonah notes that הָרָע here is masculine, unlike עַיִן רָעָה in 2:9.
הָרָע: the article on the adjective after a noun: 'the evil (eye)'.
יֵצֶר: 'impulse, inclination' (what is formed in a person). The pack links the verb יָצַר 'to form'; the noun has no entry there, so no sense is given.
בְּרִיָּה: 'creature'; with the article, 'people'.
מוֹצִיאִין: hifil participle plural with -ין, 'they take out'.

phrases.literal: 'Rabbi Yehoshua says'
'the eye the evil'; Bartenura: an eye that is not content with what it has, or one that harms another's goods
'and the impulse the evil'; יֵצֶר 'what is formed', the inclination
'and the hatred of the creatures'; Bartenura: baseless hatred, or the hatred others feel for a harsh man

phrases.english: remove a person from the world
phrases.literal: 'they take out the person from the world'; hifil plural participle of יצא

grammar: The three subjects are joined by 'and' and take the plural participle מוֹצִיאִין (hifil of יצא, with -ין, the Aramaic-style plural of Mishnaic Hebrew): 'they take a person out of the world'.
עַיִן הָרָע and יֵצֶר הָרָע both have the adjective with the article after a noun without it (the noun is definite by its qualifier); contrast עַיִן רָעָה in 2:9, with no article, 'an evil eye'.

שִׂנְאַת הַבְּרִיּוֹת is a construct chain: 'the hatred of the creatures'; whether the genitive is subjective (others' hatred) or objective (one's hatred of them) is open, as Bartenura's two readings show.
מִן הָעוֹלָם: 'from the world' means out of life; Rambam reads it as a death before one's time.
segments.note: עַיִן הָרָע: Bartenura gives two readings, the same as 'an evil eye' (discontent with one's lot) or malevolent gaze at a friend's money or children that causes harm. The English keeps the ambiguity of 'the evil eye'. שִׂנְאַת הַבְּרִיּוֹת: 'hatred of people' is likewise ambiguous: baseless hatred (Bartenura), loathing human company (Rambam, whom Bartenura reports) or the hatred a harsh man brings on himself (Bartenura's own hearing). יֵצֶר הָרָע: 'the evil impulse'; 'inclination' is equally correct.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: 'the evil eye' is like 'an evil eye': a man not content with what he has who goes after other things. Some explain it as one who casts an evil eye on his fellow's money or sons and harms him.

Bartenura: 'hatred of people' is baseless hatred. He reports that Rambam explains it as one who loathes the society of people and loves to sit alone; and he himself has heard it of a harsh man who brings on himself the hatred of people so that all hate him.

Rambam: eagerness for money, excess of desire and evil of the soul (a disease of black bile) lead a man to loathe the sight of his fellows, to prefer the company of beasts and to live in deserts and wilds; for them this is not asceticism but the evil of their desire and envy of others, and without doubt such things kill a man before his time.
Rabbeinu Yonah: 'the evil eye' means one who is not content with his portion and who looks at his fellow's wealth with an envious eye.

apparatus: No variant readings are recorded between the witnesses for this mishnah.

segments.english: Rabbi Yose says: Let your fellow's money be as dear to you as your own. Prepare yourself to learn Torah, for it is not an inheritance to you. And let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven.
segments.literal: Rabbi Yose says: let-be money-of your-fellow dear on-you like-yours; and-prepare yourself to-learn Torah, that-not-it inheritance to-you; and-all your-deeds shall-be for-name-of heaven

tokens.note: יְהִי: jussive of הָיָה, 'let ... be'.
מָמוֹן: 'money, property'.
הַתְקֵן: hifil imperative of תקן, 'make ready, put in order'.
יְרֻשָּׁה: 'inheritance'.
יִהְיוּ: 3rd plural imperfect with jussive force, 'let ... be'.

phrases.literal: 'Rabbi Yose says'

phrases.english: Let your fellow's money be as dear to you as your own
phrases.literal: 'let the money of your fellow be dear on you like yours'; same form as Rabbi Eliezer's saying in 2:10, with money for honor
'and make-fit yourself to learn Torah'; הַתְקֵן, hifil imperative of תקן

phrases.english: for it is not an inheritance to you
phrases.literal: 'that-not-it inheritance to-you'; שֶׁאֵינָהּ gives the reason

phrases.english: And let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven
phrases.literal: 'and all your deeds shall be for the name of heaven'; לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם, decisions.md

grammar: The first saying has the same frame as Rabbi Eliezer's in 2:10: יְהִי X חָבִיב עָלֶיךָ כְּשֶׁלָּךְ, with מָמוֹן in place of כָּבוֹד. כְּשֶׁלָּךְ is the preposition כּ with the genitive particle שֶׁל and the suffix: 'like yours'.
הַתְקֵן is a hifil imperative of תקן, 'make ready, fit'; with עַצְמְךָ it is reflexive, 'prepare yourself'. The infinitive construct לִלְמֹד gives the purpose.
שֶׁאֵינָהּ יְרֻשָּׁה לָךְ: אֵין with the feminine suffix -ָהּ (referring to תּוֹרָה) is the negative of a nominal clause; שֶׁ introduces the reason.
וְכָל מַעֲשֶׂיךָ יִהְיוּ: the plural 3rd person imperfect of הָיָה used as a jussive, 'let all your deeds be'.
segments.note: מָמוֹן: 'money, property' (Jastrow); the English uses 'money' to keep it apart from נְכָסִים 'property' (2:7). שֶׁאֵינָהּ יְרֻשָּׁה לָךְ: 'it is not an inheritance to you', literally 'it is not an inheritance for you': it does not pass to you from your family (Bartenura, Rabbeinu Yonah). לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם: 'for the sake of Heaven' (decisions.md); שֵׁם is Jastrow שֵׁם II 'name'.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: 'prepare yourself' means that you should not say, since my father and grandfather were wise, the Torah goes back to its lodging and I need not seek it.
Bartenura: even when you are engaged in eating and drinking and worldly occupation, intend not to give your body pleasure but to be healthy so as to do the will of your Maker.

Rambam refers to his earlier discussions, in his eighth chapter on the readiness a person must make to prepare himself for the virtues and in his fifth chapter on the saying that all your deeds should be for the sake of Heaven.
Rabbeinu Yonah: you will not attain it unless you labor in it, because it is not like the inheritance of fathers that the son receives without effort.

apparatus: 2:12.12 spelling: Vilna reads ללמוד; base לִלְמֹד.
2:12.15 spelling: Vilna reads ירושה; base יְרֻשָּׁה.
